meta.titre: Polymers: addition and condensation polymerisation, plastics and detergents

sections.contenu_markdown: Every day a trader in Douala sells "pure water" in plastic sachets, a fisherman in Limbe mends his nylon net, and a family in a village near Bafia boils palm oil and ash to make soap. Plastics, nylon and soap all belong to the chemistry of very large molecules. In the GCE O/L you are asked how a polymer forms from its monomer, how addition and condensation polymerisation differ, and why plastic waste is a problem. You are also asked how soap is made and why detergents behave differently in hard water.

items: A double bond between two carbon atoms (C=C) is found in alkenes and makes them unsaturated.
Ethene is an alkene with the formula $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}$.
An acid reacts with an alcohol or an amine to form a new compound and water.
Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions.

sections.titre: Polymers: addition polymerisation, condensation polymerisation and plastics
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **polymer** is a very large molecule made by joining many small molecules called **monomers**.

**Addition polymerisation.** Monomers that contain a C=C double bond join together. One bond of each double bond opens and the molecules link in a long chain. **Nothing is lost**, so the polymer has the same atoms as the monomers, and the chain has no C=C bonds.

$$n\ \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{(-CH_2-CH_2-)_n}$$

Ethene gives poly(ethene) (polythene), propene gives poly(propene), chloroethene gives PVC and tetrafluoroethene gives PTFE ("Teflon").

**Condensation polymerisation.** Each monomer has **two** functional groups, one at each end. When two monomers join, a small molecule, usually **water**, is lost at every link. Nylon is made from a diamine (an -$\mathrm{NH_2}$ group at each end) and a dicarboxylic acid (a -COOH group at each end); the monomers are joined by an **amide link**, -CONH-. Polyesters such as Terylene are formed from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid and have an **ester link**. Natural polymers include proteins (amide links) and starch.

| | Addition | Condensation |
|---|---|---|
| Monomers | contain C=C | two functional groups |
| Small molecule lost | no | yes (usually water) |
| Examples | polythene, PVC | nylon, polyesters, proteins |

**Plastics and the environment.** Most plastics are **not biodegradable**: bacteria cannot break them down, so waste builds up in drains and rivers. Burning plastics gives poisonous gases (PVC gives hydrogen chloride). Plastics can be reused and recycled.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question gives a monomer and asks for the polymer or the number of units.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Draw the monomer, open the double bond, and keep every other atom in place. For chloroethene $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}$ the repeat unit is $\mathrm{-CH_2-CHCl-}$. The relative molecular mass of the polymer is $n \times M_r(\text{monomer})$. Uses: polythene (bags, bottles), PVC (pipes, cable insulation), PTFE (non-stick pans).

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks for the product of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Hexane-1,6-diamine reacts with hexanedioic acid to form **nylon** and water. Each repeat unit (one diamine and one diacid) is joined by two amide links and loses two molecules of water:

$$\mathrm{H_2N(CH_2)_6NH_2 + HOOC(CH_2)_4COOH \rightarrow [-NH(CH_2)_6NH-CO(CH_2)_4CO-] + 2H_2O}$$

Nylon is strong and is used for ropes, fishing nets, clothes and toothbrush bristles.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks how soap is made or why detergents are used in hard water.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Soap** is the sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, such as sodium stearate, $\mathrm{C_{17}H_{35}COONa}$. It is made by **saponification**: boiling a fat or vegetable oil (such as palm oil) with concentrated sodium hydroxide gives soap and glycerol. The long hydrocarbon tail dissolves in grease and the charged head dissolves in water, so grease is lifted off. In hard water, soap forms an insoluble **scum** with calcium and magnesium ions: $\mathrm{2C_{17}H_{35}COONa\ +\ CaCl_{2}  \rightarrow  (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_{2}Ca\ +\ 2NaCl}$. **Soapless detergents** (made from petroleum) form soluble calcium salts, so they lather in hard water and make no scum. Detergents with branched chains are not biodegradable and cause foam on rivers; straight-chain detergents are biodegradable.

sections.enonce_markdown: Chloroethene, $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}$, is the monomer used to make PVC. (a) State the type of polymerisation and give a reason. (b) Write an equation for the formation of PVC. (c) A molecule of PVC has a relative molecular mass of 62500. Calculate the number of monomer units. (d) State one environmental problem when PVC waste is burnt. (C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)

etapes.justification: The monomer contains a C=C double bond and only the polymer is formed.
etapes.resultat_markdown: **Addition polymerisation**: the double bond opens and no small molecule is lost.

etapes.justification: Open the double bond and keep the chlorine atom on the chain.

etapes.action: Calculate the relative molecular mass of one monomer.
Find the number of monomer units.

sections.conclusion_markdown: PVC forms by **addition polymerisation**, and the molecule contains **1000** monomer units. When PVC is burnt, poisonous gases such as hydrogen chloride are produced.

items.erreur_markdown: Addition polymerisation gives off water at every link.
items.pourquoi_faux: Water is lost in condensation polymerisation. In addition polymerisation the double bonds simply open and nothing is lost.
items.correction_markdown: Addition polymers have the same atoms as the monomer; condensation polymers lose water.

items.erreur_markdown: The polymer of ethene is $\mathrm{(CH_2{=}CH_2)_n}$, with the double bond kept.
items.pourquoi_faux: The double bond is used in joining the molecules, so the chain has only single bonds.

items.erreur_markdown: Nylon is an addition polymer, like polythene.
items.pourquoi_faux: Nylon is made from monomers with two functional groups, joined by amide links with loss of water.

items.erreur_markdown: Plastics are safe to throw away because bacteria break them down.
items.pourquoi_faux: Most plastics are not biodegradable, so they stay in the environment for years.
items.correction_markdown: Reuse or recycle plastics; do not burn them, because PVC gives off poisonous gases.

items.erreur_markdown: Soap lathers well in hard water and leaves no scum.
items.pourquoi_faux: The calcium and magnesium ions in hard water form an insoluble scum with soap.
items.correction_markdown: Soapless detergents lather in hard water without scum; soap does not.

items.enonce_markdown:
Propene, $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}}$, is the monomer of poly(propene). (C = 12, H = 1)

(a) What type of polymerisation is this?

(b) Calculate the relative molecular mass of propene.

(c) Calculate the relative molecular mass of a poly(propene) molecule with 500 monomer units.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Addition polymerisation**, because propene has a C=C double bond.

(b) $M_r = 3 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 = $ **42**.

(c) $M_r = 500 \times 42 = $ **21000**.

items.enonce_markdown:
Nylon is made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid.

(a) What type of polymerisation is used?

(b) Name the small molecule that is lost.

(c) Name the link that joins the monomers.

(d) Each repeat unit is made from one molecule of the diamine and one of the diacid, and loses two molecules of the small molecule. Calculate the mass of the small molecule lost when 0.50 mol of repeat units forms. (H = 1, O = 16)

(e) State one use of nylon.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Condensation polymerisation**.

(b) **Water**.

(c) The **amide link**, -CONH-.

(d) $n(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 0.50 \times 2 = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $M(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 18$, so the mass is **18 g**.

(e) **Ropes** (or fishing nets, clothes).

items.enonce_markdown:
Sodium stearate, $\mathrm{C_{17}H_{35}COONa}$, is a soap. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23, Ca = 40, Cl = 35.5)

(a) Write the equation for the reaction of this soap with calcium chloride in hard water.

(b) Calculate the mass of calcium chloride that reacts completely with 3.06 g of the soap.

(c) Explain why a soapless detergent does not form scum in hard water.

(d) Explain why detergents with branched chains harm rivers.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{2C_{17}H_{35}COONa\ +\ CaCl_{2}  \rightarrow  (C_{17}H_{35}COO)_{2}Ca\ +\ 2NaCl}$

(b) $M(\mathrm{C_{17}H_{35}COONa}) = 18 \times 12 + 35 + 32 + 23 = 306$, so $n = \dfrac{3.06}{306} = 0.010\ \mathrm{mol}$. The ratio soap : $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ is 2 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{CaCl_2}) = 0.0050\ \mathrm{mol}$. $M(\mathrm{CaCl_2}) = 111$, so $m = 0.0050 \times 111 = $ **0.555 g**.

(c) The calcium and magnesium salts of soapless detergents are soluble in water, so no insoluble scum forms.

(d) Branched-chain detergents are not biodegradable, so bacteria cannot break them down and they cause persistent foam on rivers.

items_markdown: Addition polymerisation: monomers with C=C join with nothing lost, and the polymer has no double bond (polythene, PVC).
Condensation polymerisation: monomers with two functional groups join and lose water at each link (nylon with amide links, polyesters with ester links).
Number of units in a polymer: $n = M_r(\text{polymer}) / M_r(\text{monomer})$ for an addition polymer.
Most plastics are not biodegradable; burning some gives poisonous gases such as hydrogen chloride.
Soap is made by boiling fat or oil with sodium hydroxide (saponification); it forms scum in hard water, whereas soapless detergents do not.
